title: Georgia Unclaimed Property: Search and Claim Guide (November 2026)
summary: See how Georgia families can search for and claim unclaimed property left by a deceased relative, with 2026 documentation requirements.
body_markdown:
During estate settlement in Georgia, a deceased relative may have unclaimed property held by the state, such as wages, savings accounts, or insurance payments. Whether a claim can be paid depends on proof of death and the claimant's legal authority to act for the estate. This guide explains key points for families and executors to be aware of, including: how property becomes unclaimed, who has authority to claim, how to search by name, what documents are required, and more.


**Key Takeaways**


- Georgia’s official unclaimed property search is free and uses the deceased person’s name.
- Estate claims typically need a certified death certificate and court-issued proof of authority.
- Georgia has no claim deadline. Families can claim directly without paying a finder.
- Georgia DOR says most claims are paid within 30 days; processing can take up to 90 days.
- Elayne requests prior years’ tax transcripts with IRS authorization to help locate estate assets.


## What Georgia Unclaimed Property Is


Georgia unclaimed property is money and other assets turned over to the state for safekeeping until claimed. The Georgia Department of Revenue administers the program under the Disposition of Unclaimed Property Act. According to Forbes Advisor, Georgia holds $3.3 billion in unclaimed money.


The program covers:


- Unclaimed wages and savings accounts
- Customer refunds and insurance payments
- Shares of stock and U.S. savings bonds
- Escrow funds
- Contents of safe deposit boxes


A deceased relative’s name may appear in these records. Georgia permits[searches for accounts after a death](https://www.elayne.com/resources/find-hidden-accounts-after-death) on behalf of an estate.

## How Property Becomes Unclaimed in Georgia


Banks and other businesses must report and transfer property after a set period of inactivity, called dormancy.


Property or notice requirement Georgia rule


Most property 5 years of inactivity


Unpaid wages 1 year


Owner notice for $50 to $10,000 First-class mail


Owner notice above $10,000 Certified mail


The dormancy periods and mailing thresholds above are outlined in[Georgia DOR’s holder filing guidance](https://dor.georgia.gov/document/document/holder-annual-filing-report-information/download) ; these mailing rules apply beginning July 1, 2026. Georgia holds unclaimed property indefinitely, so families have no deadline to claim it.


## Who Has the Authority to Claim on Behalf of a Deceased Relative


Anyone can search Georgia unclaimed property listings by name. Claiming for a deceased relative requires proof of authority, usually Letters Testamentary or Letters of Administration showing the claimant’s court appointment as executor or administrator. Being named executor in a will does not, by itself, grant court authority.


A surviving spouse may qualify to claim without full probate, depending on the value and applicable claim rules, as outlined in this[unclaimed inheritance search guide](https://www.elayne.com/resources/unclaimed-property-and-inheritance-search-guide) .


Search and claim information includes the deceased person’s name, Social Security number and/or the estate’s Federal Employer Identification Number, plus documentation supporting the claimant’s authority.


## How to Search for a Deceased Relative's Unclaimed Property in Georgia


Georgia’s official unclaimed property search is free. No account is required to search; registration comes when submitting a claim.


1. The search begins with the deceased relative’s name. Former names and common spelling variations can help locate records.
2. Adding a city narrows results when several people share a name.
3. Potential matches are compared with family records before a claim is started.


The database contains property reported to Georgia. For relatives who lived in multiple states, other state unclaimed property programs may hold separate records.


## Searching Beyond Georgia: Other States and National Databases


A Georgia unclaimed property search may not cover everything. Searches generally follow the owner's last known location; the holder's state can matter when owner information is missing. Former residences and account history can guide searches elsewhere.


- MissingMoney.com offers a free multi-state search endorsed by NAUPA and the National Association of State Treasurers. For searches involving New York City, the[NYC unclaimed money guide](https://www.elayne.com/resources/find-nyc-unclaimed-money) is a separate, location-specific resource.
- USA.gov's unclaimed money directory points to federal programs, including tax refunds and unclaimed benefits. Refunds owed to someone who died require the applicable estate claim process.


Unclaimed property programs returned over $5 billion in fiscal year 2023, according to NAUPA.


## What Documentation Is Required to File an Estate Claim


A Georgia unclaimed property estate claim typically requires:


- A completed Georgia unclaimed property claim form.
- A certified copy of[the death certificate](https://www.usa.gov/death-certificate) .
- Court-issued proof of authority to act for the estate, such as Letters Testamentary or Letters of Administration.
- The estate’s Employer Identification Number, if issued, instead of or alongside the deceased person’s Social Security number, as required by the claim instructions.


For a surviving spouse claiming jointly owned property, a death certificate and proof of marriage support the claim, similar to the documentation involved in[locating unclaimed property from a deceased parent](https://www.elayne.com/resources/locating-unclaimed-property-parent) . Claim-specific instructions determine whether further evidence is required.

## How Elayne Helps Families Find Accounts Before They Reach the State


Unclaimed property programs hold only the accounts that businesses have already turned over to the state. Under Georgia’s dormancy rules, most property is transferred to the state after 5 years of inactivity, and unpaid wages after 1 year. Until then, many accounts tied to a person who died remain with the original bank, insurer, employer, or plan administrator and do not appear in a state database. Elayne Asset Search checks the sources that record these accounts, starting with IRS tax transcripts and an Equifax credit report.


Elayne holds IRS authorization to request a person’s IRS tax transcripts for the prior 10 years. An IRS tax transcript is not a tax return. An IRS tax transcript lists what banks, employers, insurers, and retirement account custodians reported to the IRS about the person, such as interest paid, retirement distributions, and wages. Each reported item points to an institution that may hold an account. For example, a bank that reported interest or a retirement account custodian that reported a distribution appears in the transcripts even when no statement is in the person’s papers.


Elayne also requests the person’s Equifax credit report, which lists open accounts, credit cards, loans, and other debts in the person’s name.


The search then checks more than 100 other sources, including:


- Life insurance locators, which cover in-force and lapsed policies
- The federal pension registry, which lists unclaimed pensions from terminated plans
- The national unclaimed property database and state unclaimed property searches
- Property and vehicle records
- Crypto exchange accounts, when tax transcripts or the estate record point to crypto
- Veterans benefits and VA life insurance, when the estate record shows veteran status


Each finding is added to an estate inventory along with the institution that reported the finding. The inventory groups findings into retirement accounts, bank and brokerage accounts, life insurance, property, business interests, and debts. A one-on-one call with an Estate Expert walks through the findings. If the search finds nothing new, the estate record still shows whether the estate owes the IRS anything, which debts are open, and that the search was completed.


Legal authority determines how much of the search can run. Portions of the search can begin before a court appoints an executor or administrator, and court-issued legal authority, such as Letters Testamentary or Letters of Administration, allows the full search. The appointed executor or administrator holds the authority to act for the estate. The executor reviews the findings, and the estate’s attorney advises on claims and distributions.


A person who lived in several states may have records in each state, as covered in guides on[finding money in Florida after a death](https://www.elayne.com/resources/find-loved-ones-money-florida) and a[Maryland unclaimed property search](https://www.elayne.com/resources/maryland-unclaimed-money-search) .


Asset Search costs $3,000 in total, which includes Estate Setup. Asset Search is an eligible estate expense, paid from the estate account or reimbursed by the estate.[See how Elayne can help families settle an estate](https://www.elayne.com/) .


## FAQ


### What do MissingMoney.com and USA.gov cover?


MissingMoney.com helps locate property held by participating states, while USA.gov links to separate federal programs for refunds and benefits. A negative Georgia result does not rule out money elsewhere or accounts still held by financial institutions.


### What if a deceased relative’s name appears in Georgia Department of Revenue listings but the match is unconfirmed?


A matching name alone is not enough to prove the property belonged to the deceased relative. Old statements, prior cities of residence, and records naming the reporting business can help support the connection. If details remain unclear, the Georgia Department of Revenue can explain what evidence the claim requires.


### What if Georgia Department of Revenue unclaimed property is found after a deceased relative’s estate has closed?


The funds may still be claimed, but the closed estate can affect who has authority to receive them. The Georgia Department of Revenue can clarify its documentation requirements, and a probate attorney can advise whether further court action is needed before payment or distribution.


### What information is needed to search Georgia unclaimed property on behalf of an estate?


A search on behalf of an estate begins with the deceased person's name, Social Security number, and/or the estate's Federal Employer Identification Number. A general public search uses a name alone, and adding a city narrows the results.
